title: Extraordinary Utilities
description: Extraordinary utilities are the narrow exception under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(2)(ii) letting certain utility costs count as qualified research supplies.

Only incremental costs demanded by the special character of qualified research qualify; routine facility utilities remain excluded overhead, and square-footage allocations are insufficient.

body.text: Extraordinary utilities are the narrow exception under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(b)(2)(ii) that lets U.S. taxpayers claim certain electricity, gas, or water costs as qualified research supplies for the federal R&D tax credit under IRC Section 41. Only incremental costs demanded by the special character of qualified research qualify; routine facility utilities remain excluded overhead, and square-footage allocations are insufficient.
Executive Summary: The Narrow Qualification Exception for Research Utilities

Within the statutory architecture of the U.S. federal Research and Development (R&D) tax credit under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41, utility expenses occupy a heavily restricted compliance category. Under the default rule codified in Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(b)(2)(i), expenditures for utilities—including electricity, natural gas, and water—incurred in the operation of a building or facility in which qualified research is performed are classified as general and administrative (G&A) overhead expenses. Because indirect research expenditures and G&A overhead are categorically excluded from in-house research expenses under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(b)(1), routine utility costs such as standard building illumination, ambient heating, and general office or laboratory climate control cannot be included in Qualified Research Expenses (QREs).

Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(b)(2)(ii) establishes the sole regulatory exception to this general disallowance by permitting the inclusion of "certain extraordinary utilities". When a taxpayer demonstrates that the "special character" of a qualified research activity (QRA) directly necessitated utility consumption far exceeding standard facility operation, those "additional extraordinary expenditures" are recharacterized as qualified costs of "supplies used in the conduct of qualified research". Rather than subsidizing routine physical infrastructure, this exception targets high-energy, capital-intensive experimental processes—such as powering high-output lasers, nuclear research apparatus, plasma etching tools, cryogenic systems, or industrial pilot furnaces—where extreme energy draw is physically inseparable from resolving technological uncertainty.

Because the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) explicitly rejects simplistic cost-apportionment techniques such as square-footage comparisons between research and administrative buildings, claiming Extraordinary Utilities requires a rigorous convergence of financial accounting and empirical engineering substantiation. Taxpayers must isolate the exact incremental load and temporal duration of qualified experimental usage from routine facility operations while simultaneously managing downstream tax interactions across IRC Section 280C(c) deduction and capital-account reductions, IRC Section 174 and Section 174A research and experimental (R&E) capitalization and expensing regimes, and IRC Section 861 international expense apportionment.
Statutory and Regulatory Architecture of Qualified Supply Expenses
IRC Section 41 Qualified Research Expense Categories

Codified under IRC Section 41, the Credit for Increasing Research Activities functions as an incremental, dollar-for-dollar general business tax credit offset under IRC Section 38 designed to incentivize domestic research and development expenditure within the United States. Under IRC Section 41(a)(1), the regular research credit equals 20% of the excess of the taxpayer's QREs for the taxable year over a statutory base amount, complemented by a 20% credit for basic research payments determined under IRC Section 41(e)(1)(A) per IRC Section 41(a)(2) and a 20% credit for amounts paid or incurred to an energy research consortium for energy research per IRC Section 41(a)(3). The computation of the credit depends on the aggregation of eligible QREs paid or incurred by the taxpayer during the taxable year in carrying on a trade or business across strictly defined statutory categories.

Under IRC Section 41(b)(1)–(3), total QREs comprise the sum of in-house research expenses and contract research expenses. Specifically, in-house research expenses under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(A) encompass taxable wages (as defined in IRC Section 3401(a), excluding amounts taken into account in determining the work opportunity credit under IRC Section 51(a)) paid or incurred to an employee for performing qualified services—defined in IRC Section 41(b)(2)(B) as engaging in qualified research, or engaging in the direct supervision or direct support of research activities which constitute qualified research (with all of an individual's services treated as qualified services if "substantially all" of the services performed by that individual for the taxpayer during the taxable year consist of qualified services). In-house research expenses also include any amount paid or incurred for supplies used in the conduct of qualified research under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(A)(ii), as well as any amount paid or incurred to another person for the right to use (time-sharing) computers in the conduct of qualified research under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(A)(iii) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(b)(4) (such as external cloud service provider server leasing, provided the computer is owned and operated by someone other than the taxpayer, located off the taxpayer's premises, and the taxpayer is not the primary user of the computer). Complementing in-house expenses, contract research expenses under IRC Section 41(b)(3) encompass a statutory percentage—generally 65% under IRC Section 41(b)(3)(A) (increased to 75% for amounts paid to qualified tax-exempt scientific research consortia under IRC Section 41(b)(3)(C), and 100% for amounts paid to eligible small businesses, institutions of higher education, or federal laboratories for energy research under IRC Section 41(b)(3)(D))—of amounts paid or incurred to non-employees for qualified research performed on the taxpayer's behalf. Because IRC Section 41(b) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(b)(1) establish an exclusive list of qualifying in-house expenditures, expenditures for Extraordinary Utilities qualify exclusively under the "supplies" category of in-house research expenses.
Statutory Definition of Supplies and the Depreciable Property Exclusion

Under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(C) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(b), the term "supplies" encompasses any tangible property other than (i) land or improvements to land, and (ii) property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation, that is used or consumed in the conduct of qualified research. Under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(b)(1), supplies are used in the conduct of qualified research if they are used in the performance of qualified services (as defined in IRC Section 41(b)(2)(B), but without regard to the last sentence thereof concerning the "substantially all" rule) by an employee of the taxpayer or by a person acting in a capacity similar to that of an employee. In typical laboratory or manufacturing settings, qualified supplies consist of raw materials, chemical reagents, electronic components consumed during prototype fabrication, and scrap material generated during destructive testing.

The statutory exclusion of depreciable tangible property under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(C)(ii) removes capital expenditures—such as the acquisition cost of long-lived laboratory machinery, environmental testing chambers, electron microscopes, and semiconductor lithography systems—from the QRE base, as those capital costs are recovered separately through depreciation deductions. Judicial precedents strictly police the boundary between consumable supplies and non-qualifying production or depreciable assets. In TG Missouri Corp. v. Commissioner, 133 T.C. 278 (2009), the U.S. Tax Court held that custom production molds fabricated by a taxpayer for a third-party customer that took title and ownership were not property subject to an allowance for depreciation in the taxpayer's hands and could therefore qualify as supplies under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(C). Conversely, in Union Carbide Corp. & Subsidiaries v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2009-50, aff'd, 697 F.3d 104, the courts disallowed supply claims for raw materials used during full-scale commercial production runs where the taxpayer would have incurred those material costs to produce salable goods regardless of whether experimental process trials were conducted.

Concurrently, Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(b)(1) and § 1.41-2(b)(2)(i) exclude expenditures for indirect research and general and administrative services, establishing the baseline rule that amounts paid or incurred for utilities such as water, electricity, and natural gas used in the building in which qualified research is performed—even a facility dedicated exclusively to research—are treated as G&A expenses and do not constitute qualified supplies.

body.text: Factual Correction Regarding Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2 vs. § 1.41-2(b)(2)(ii)

In federal tax law, Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2 defines research or experimental expenditures in the experimental or laboratory sense—including the definition of a "pilot model" under Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(4) as any representation or model of a product produced to evaluate and resolve uncertainty concerning the product during its development or improvement—for purposes of IRC Section 174 and Section 174A capitalization and deductibility, while excluding post-uncertainty production costs under § 1.174-2(a)(2) and ordinary quality control testing under § 1.174-2(a)(6).

Although satisfying the IRC Section 174 / Section 174A definition is the first requirement of "qualified research" under IRC Section 41(d)(1)(A), not all research expenditures eligible under IRC Section 174 or Section 174A qualify as QREs for the IRC Section 41 credit computation. As the IRS Research Credit Audit Techniques Guide (ATG) notes, examiners consult Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2 when scrutinizing prototype expenses to determine whether a prototype or its subcomponents constitute property of a character subject to an allowance for depreciation. However, Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(b)(2)(ii) is the specific controlling regulation that admits extraordinary utilities into the IRC Section 41 QRE supply base. Compliance documentation must therefore cite Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(b)(2)(ii) when substantiating Extraordinary Utilities as qualified supplies for the research tax credit, while referencing Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(4) to establish that the underlying pilot model activity constitutes experimental research rather than commercial production.
Economic Counterbalance for Capital-Intensive Innovation

The regulatory exception in Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(b)(2)(ii) serves a vital structural function within federal innovation policy by preserving technological neutrality across disparate industrial sectors. In software development or clinical trial management, research expenditures are overwhelmingly concentrated in employee wages, allowing taxpayers to capture the vast majority of their innovation investment within the wage QRE category. Conversely, in capital-intensive sectors such as aerospace engineering, semiconductor fabrication, metallurgy, pharmaceuticals, and advanced materials science, innovation relies on capital-intensive equipment whose purchase price is barred from QREs by the depreciable property exclusion under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(C)(ii).

If federal regulations excluded both the depreciable acquisition cost of specialized research apparatus and the massive electrical, thermal, or cryogenic energy required to operate that apparatus during experimentation, the IRC Section 41 credit would systematically penalize hardware- and energy-intensive domestic research. By permitting taxpayers to claim the incremental, extraordinary utility costs directly demanded by specialized research equipment, Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(b)(2)(ii) partially offsets the capital asset exclusion and aligns the credit base with the true operational cost of physical experimentation.
Regulatory Mechanics of the Extraordinary Utilities Exception
The Dual-Prong Burden of Proof

To reclassify a utility expenditure from excluded G&A overhead to a qualified supply under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(b)(2)(ii), the taxpayer bears the affirmative burden of establishing two distinct factual elements. First, the taxpayer must establish the "special character" of the qualified research by demonstrating that the underlying research activity possesses unique technical or experimental characteristics that inherently demand extreme utility consumption. The energy, water, or gas draw must be directly linked to resolving technological uncertainty concerning capability, method, or appropriate design through a process of experimentation under IRC Section 41(d), rather than supporting routine manufacturing, commercial batch production, or standard quality control testing. Second, the taxpayer must substantiate "additional extraordinary expenditures" by proving that the claimed utility costs represent incremental, extraordinary amounts paid or incurred above and beyond the baseline utility consumption required for general facility operations, demanded solely by the execution of the qualified research.

Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(b)(2)(ii) illustrates this boundary by contrasting non-qualifying amounts paid for electricity used for general laboratory lighting and climate control with qualifying amounts paid for electricity used in the operation of high-energy equipment for qualified research, such as laser or nuclear research. Only the incremental portion of the utility expenditure proven to be both additional and extraordinary qualifies as a supply used in the conduct of qualified research.
Temporal and Functional Segregation in Mixed-Use Facilities

A critical operational complication arises because industrial and laboratory facilities rarely operate exclusively for qualified research twenty-four hours a day. Frequently, a single specialized testing bay or clean room utilizes high-energy apparatus for a qualified experiment during a discrete window—such as four hours of high-temperature alloy stress testing or plasma deposition—and subsequently reverts to non-qualified commercial production, routine calibration, or standard quality assurance testing for the remainder of the operating shift.

In such mixed-use environments, the utility consumption of the facility is legally "extraordinary" only during the exact temporal interval in which the qualified research activity is physically executing and drawing the exceptional energy load. Averaging utility expenditures across an entire billing cycle or across total building floor area improperly blends high-intensity experimental energy spikes with low-intensity commercial or administrative usage. Furthermore, consistent with the principle in Union Carbide Corp. v. Commissioner, baseline utility loads that a facility would have incurred for commercial production regardless of experimentation are ineligible as research supplies. Consequently, compliant cost capture requires both functional segregation (isolating the specific research equipment from general building systems) and temporal segregation (isolating the exact hours of qualified experimentation from non-qualified equipment operation).
Hypothetical Worked Example: Foundry Pilot Model and Mixed-Use Utility Segregation

A domestic metallurgical manufacturer operates an industrial facility that incurs a total monthly electricity invoice of $50,000. Routine facility illumination accounts for $1,000, while standard commercial production and baseline HVAC loads account for an additional $29,000, resulting in $30,000 (or 60% of the monthly utility bill) attributable to general overhead and non-research operations. During a 30-day testing cycle, the taxpayer operates an electric arc blast furnace to test an experimental alloy ("Pilot Model" under Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(4)) designed to resolve technological uncertainty regarding high-temperature structural fatigue.

Assuming the experimental blast furnace draws a verified continuous operating load of 2,000 kW during experimental runs and operates for 100 hours of qualified experimentation during the billing period at a contracted industrial electricity rate of $0.10 per kWh, the engineering load and temporal verification yield the following extraordinary consumption:
200,000 kWh × $0.10/kWh = $20,000 Extraordinary Research Utility Expenditure
Out of the $50,000 total monthly utility invoice, the extraordinary research intensity represents exactly 40%:
$20,000 Extraordinary Research Utility ÷ $50,000 Total Monthly Bill = 40%

Only the $20,000 incremental cost directly attributable to the blast furnace during qualified experimental runs is included in the IRC Section 41 QRE supply base, while the remaining $30,000 is excluded as general overhead under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(b)(2)(i). Furthermore, under IRC Section 280C(c)(1), if the taxpayer claims the full research tax credit on the $20,000 Extraordinary Utility QRE (assuming, for hypothetical illustration, an incremental credit yield of 15%, or $3,000, attributable to these supplies) without electing the reduced credit under IRC Section 280C(c)(2), the taxpayer's deductible domestic R&E expenditure (under IRC Section 174A(a) for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024) or capitalizable IRC Section 174 Specified Research or Experimental (SRE) expenditure basis (for 2022–2024 taxable years, or under an IRC Section 174A(c) capitalization election) must be reduced by the $3,000 credit claimed, leaving $17,000 of net deductible or capitalizable supply cost to prevent a double tax benefit. Alternatively, if the taxpayer timely elects the reduced credit under IRC Section 280C(c)(2) on its original return (Form 6765, Item A), the $3,000 credit is reduced by the maximum corporate tax rate of 21% under IRC Section 11(b) (a $630 reduction), resulting in a net credit of $2,370 (79% of $3,000) while preserving the full $20,000 deduction or capitalizable basis.

body.text: IRS Audit Scrutiny and Substantiation Standards
IRS Audit Techniques Guide (ATG) Examination Standards

Because Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(b)(2)(ii) represents the sole regulatory departure from the general disallowance of utility expenses, IRS examiners subject Extraordinary Utilities claims to heightened audit scrutiny. According to the IRS Audit Techniques Guide (ATG) for the Credit for Increasing Research Activities (IRC § 41), an examiner's review focuses not merely on verifying that the utility invoice was paid, but fundamentally on evaluating the technical and engineering justification proving that the consumption was extraordinary and necessitated by the special character of the qualified research.

Simultaneously, the IRS ATG establishes procedural safeguards governing audit disallowances: if an examiner denies a taxpayer's Extraordinary Utilities claim on grounds of inadequate substantiation, the examiner must explicitly document the examination methodology and provide a detailed written analysis explaining why the taxpayer's supporting evidence was unreliable, insufficient, irrelevant, or misleading. Specifically, under Section (2) (Substantiation and Documentation) of the IRS Research Credit ATG, detailing the examiner's methodology begins with identifying the taxpayer's cost accounting system, explaining why that system represents (or would normally represent) the best evidence, and identifying the records maintained (or not maintained) and the specific Information Document Requests (IDRs) issued. Furthermore, if an examiner does not request documentation necessary to evaluate an issue, that evidence is presumed immaterial to the conclusion reached, whereas if new documentation on a material requested issue is later submitted at the IRS Independent Office of Appeals, Internal Revenue Manual (IRM) 8.2.1.2.2 requires Appeals to return the documentation to the examiner for evaluation. This reciprocal evidentiary standard underscores that a well-structured, engineering-backed substantiation package significantly strengthens a taxpayer's audit defense, whereas generalized estimates invite a formal, technically detailed disallowance.
Explicit Rejection of Square-Footage Allocations

A cornerstone of IRS examination policy in this area is the categorical rejection of spatial allocation methodologies. Both IRS guidance and the Research Credit ATG explicitly state under the Extraordinary Utilities heading that "merely comparing the square footage electricity use in an administrative building with a research facility is insufficient" to establish the extraordinary nature of a utility expenditure under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(b)(2)(ii).

Square-footage comparisons fail regulatory scrutiny because energy consumption in advanced research facilities is highly asymmetric and localized within specific pieces of apparatus—such as clean-room air handlers, high-density server racks, cryogenic chillers, or plasma reactors—rather than distributed uniformly across floor space. Spatial averaging conflates baseline ambient building loads with localized experimental spikes and fails to distinguish between hours when research apparatus is idle, hours when it is used for commercial production, and hours when it is engaged in qualified experimentation.
The Five Pillars of Defensible Audit Documentation

To overcome the insufficiency of spatial allocations and satisfy the IRS ATG burden of proof, taxpayers must maintain a contemporaneous substantiation file integrating accounting records with empirical engineering evidence.

body.text: When physical sub-meters are not installed on shared utility lines—such as when a central industrial chiller supplies cooling water to both an R&D clean room and a commercial assembly floor—the Allocation Methodology Paper must rely on verifiable engineering metrics. Defensible metrics include proportional thermal cooling loads (BTUs or tons of refrigeration) calculated by professional engineers from equipment nameplate ratings multiplied by logged QRA operating hours, paralleling the rigorous allocation standards required for funded research contracts.
Cross-Provision Financial and International Tax Linkages

Claiming Extraordinary Utilities under IRC Section 41 does not occur in a statutory vacuum; expanding the domestic QRE supply base triggers mandatory mechanical adjustments across domestic capitalization and deductibility statutes as well as international income-sourcing regimes.
Interaction with IRC Section 280C(c) and IRC Section 174 / Section 174A Capitalization and Expensing

All QREs claimed under IRC Section 41—including Extraordinary Utilities—are governed by the anti-double-benefit rules of IRC Section 280C(c), which have evolved across three statutory eras. Historically, for taxable years beginning before January 1, 2022, when research expenditures were immediately deductible under former IRC Section 174, former IRC Section 280C(c)(1) required a taxpayer claiming the full research credit to reduce its otherwise allowable IRC Section 174 deduction by the exact dollar amount of the research credit claimed, unless the taxpayer elected a reduced credit under IRC Section 280C(c)(2).

For taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, and before January 1, 2025, the statutory landscape shifted substantially under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA, Public Law 115-97, § 13206) with the mandatory capitalization and amortization of Specified Research or Experimental (SRE) expenditures (5-year ratable amortization for domestic SRE expenditures and 15-year amortization for foreign SRE expenditures, beginning at the midpoint of the taxable year) under amended IRC Section 174. Under the TCJA text of IRC Section 280C(c)(1), if the IRC Section 41(a)(1) research credit for the taxable year exceeded the amount allowable as a deduction for qualified research expenses or basic research expenses, the amount chargeable to a capital account (as capitalized SRE expenditures under IRC Section 174) had to be reduced by the amount of such excess.

Subsequently, on July 4, 2025, Congress enacted the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA, Public Law 119-21), which in Section 70302 added IRC Section 174A and amended IRC Section 174, IRC Section 41(d), and IRC Section 280C(c)(1) for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024. Under IRC Section 174A(a), taxpayers may once again immediately deduct domestic research or experimental expenditures in the taxable year paid or incurred, or irrevocably elect under IRC Section 174A(c)(1) (by the return filing deadline, including extensions) to capitalize and amortize domestic R&E expenditures ratably over not less than 60 months, while IRC Section 174 is narrowed exclusively to foreign R&E expenditures (which remain subject to 15-year capitalization and amortization, with no deduction or reduction to amount realized allowed on the disposition, retirement, or abandonment of foreign research property after May 12, 2025). Concurrently, OBBBA Section 70302(b)(2)(B) amended IRC Section 280C(c)(1) to provide directly that the domestic research or experimental expenditures (as defined in IRC Section 174A(b)) otherwise taken into account as a deduction or charged to a capital account must be reduced by the amount of the credit allowed under IRC Section 41(a), while explicitly stating that this amendment creates no inference regarding how IRC Section 280C(c) applied for taxable years beginning before January 1, 2025. The irrevocable election for a reduced research credit under IRC Section 280C(c)(2) (reducing the credit by the 21% maximum corporate tax rate under IRC Section 11(b) to 79% of the full credit on a timely filed original return on Form 6765, Item A) remained unchanged. For unamortized 2022–2024 domestic Section 174 SRE balances, OBBBA Section 70302(f) and IRS Revenue Procedure 2025-28 (modifying Revenue Procedure 2025-23) established transition paths, including a small-business retroactive election window (which closed on July 6, 2026) and automatic accounting method changes via Form 3115 (such as Designated Change Numbers 265 and 273 discussed in practitioner guidance) allowing taxpayers to recover remaining unamortized 2022–2024 domestic SRE amounts in 2025 or ratably over 2025–2026. Tax compliance teams must coordinate their IRC Section 41 Extraordinary Utilities claims directly with their IRC Section 174 and Section 174A schedules and Form 6765 Section 280C(c) elections to ensure consistent basis and deduction tracking.
International Tax Apportionment Under IRC Section 861 and Treasury Regulation § 1.861-17

For multinational enterprises (MNEs), claiming Extraordinary Utilities produces a critical second-order effect on international tax liability through the expense allocation and apportionment rules of IRC Section 861. Under Treasury Regulation § 1.861-17, research and experimental (R&E) expenditures—which encompass domestic R&D deductions and amortization deductions—are allocable to gross income connected with relevant three-digit Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) code product categories (with aggregation permitted within the same two-digit SIC Major Group) and must be apportioned between domestic-source income (the residual grouping) and foreign-source income (the statutory grouping). Under the 2020 Final Regulations (T.D. 9922), Treasury eliminated the optional gross income method for apportioning R&E expenses, mandating the use of the sales method, under which 50% of R&E expenditures performed more than 50% in the United States is apportioned exclusively to U.S.-source gross income and the remaining R&E pool is apportioned ratably based on relative domestic and foreign sales within the SIC product category.

When an MNE increases its domestic R&D expenditure pool by identifying and claiming Extraordinary Utilities, a proportional share of that enlarged R&E expense pool must frequently be apportioned against foreign-source gross income when computing the taxpayer's Foreign Tax Credit (FTC) limitation. Apportioning additional domestic R&E expense against foreign-source income reduces the MNE's net foreign-source taxable income. Because the allowable FTC limitation is bounded by the ratio of net foreign-source taxable income to worldwide taxable income, a large domestic Extraordinary Utilities claim can compress the MNE's FTC limitation and create stranded foreign tax credits that cannot be utilized. Consequently, for multinational taxpayers operating near their FTC limitation threshold, claiming Extraordinary Utilities requires integrated domestic-and-international tax modeling to verify that the domestic IRC Section 41 credit gain exceeds any resulting foreign tax credit disallowance.
Modernization Imperatives and Regulatory Recommendations

The prevailing regulatory framework in Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(b)(2)(ii)—anchored in legacy industrial examples such as "laser or nuclear research"—predates the rise of computational research and leaves substantial gray areas that breed audit controversy.
Clarifying High-Performance Computing (HPC) and Proprietary Data Center Energy Costs

Contemporary R&D across artificial intelligence, machine learning model training, bioinformatics, and computational fluid dynamics relies on massive computational power. While payments to external Cloud Service Providers (CSPs) for server space used in qualified development are recognized under the computer rental QRE provisions of IRC Section 41(b)(2)(A)(iii) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(b)(4) (when the computer is owned and operated by a third party, located off the taxpayer's premises, and the taxpayer is not the primary user), the substantial electricity and specialized liquid- or air-cooling utility costs incurred by a taxpayer operating an in-house, proprietary R&D data center face regulatory ambiguity under the legacy "laser or nuclear research" supply examples. Treasury and the IRS should issue formal guidance confirming that electrical and cooling utilities consumed by dedicated, high-density proprietary R&D computing infrastructure qualify as Extraordinary Utilities under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(b)(2)(ii).
Establishing Quantitative Safe Harbor Thresholds via Energy Usage Intensity

Currently, proving that utility consumption is "extraordinary" and demanded by the "special character" of research relies on qualitative, subjective assessments during IRS examinations. Treasury and the IRS should supplement the qualitative standard with an objective, quantitative safe harbor or rebuttable presumption based on verifiable Energy Usage Intensity (EUI)—measured in kilowatt-hours per unit of volume or floor area—where consumption in a dedicated research zone exceeds a defined multiple, specifically 3× to 5× (3.0× to 5.0×), of documented standard commercial or industrial building benchmarks.
Formalizing a Three-Tiered Allocation Revenue Procedure for Mixed-Use Facilities

Because existing IRS guidance operates negatively by rejecting square-footage comparisons without codifying approved alternatives, taxpayers face persistent audit disputes over engineering estimates. The IRS should publish a formal Revenue Procedure establishing a three-tier hierarchy of accepted allocation methodologies in descending order of evidentiary preference: first, Direct Sub-Metering on specific high-energy research apparatus; second, Engineering Load Calculations combining verifiable equipment nameplate power ratings with contemporaneous QRA utilization logs; and third, Time-Based Allocation tied directly to documented QRA execution schedules where physical sub-metering or load isolation is technically infeasible.
